A major deleveraging wave is sweeping across the US ETF market:

The notional value of the 200 largest US ETFs has declined -$100 billion, or -20%, over the last month, to ~$400 billion, the lowest since May.

This metric represents total market exposure provided by these ETFs, including the impact of leverage. 

For example, a leveraged ETF with $100 billion in assets and 2x leverage would provide $200 billion in notional exposure.

This follows a +$200 billion, or +67%, surge since the March 30th market bottom.

By comparison, the notional value declined -$130 billion, or -37%, from its November 2024 peak to the April 2025 bottom.

Despite the recent decline, leveraged ETF exposure remains +100% above the peak level seen during the 2021 meme stock frenzy.

Leverage is catalyzing severe volatility.

.@LassieAI co-founder and CEO Steijn Pelle says small businesses like doctors' offices should run themselves:

"The busy work is done by agents."

"We want to build agents for the business that then will interface with the personal agent of a consumer."

"It needs to really work, and the onboarding needs to be as simple as onboarding on Coinbase or Stripe."

"All small businesses at an abstract level have a system of record they need to read and write into. They all have customers... it's interacting and transacting around payments. You need to book appointments."

"The end goal is if we served all the doctor offices, that we help all the small businesses across the world."

@steijnpelle

tweets.text:
BUY WHEN THE MAIN CHARACTER GETS LIQUIDATED

This morning we executed our largest single-day rotation since $NODE launched, selling ~750bps of defensive, lower-beta names and adding aggressively to many of the AI infrastructure miners that Situational Awareness LP was forced to dump before the open.

Leopold Aschenbrenner built one of the last year's best-performing funds in the world on the same thesis we've been running: AI needs power, and the BTC miners are among the cheapest ways to play it. Unfortunately, 4x leverage turned a bad July into margin calls and the liquidation of his public book.

(Pro tip: if you don't take the other side of forced, leveraged sellers when your favorite stocks become divorced from fundamentals, your longer time horizon, lack of leverage, and diversification benefits lose their edge.)

When $NODE launched a year ago our thesis was that diversification and avoiding undue leverage would generate a higher Sharpe than peers. That thesis has largely played out. Since inception $NODE +46% vs. Bitcoin -37% and our DAPP index +44% (at much higher vol). We might have missed some upside, but we got no margin calls. Through yesterday we were roughly flat on the year.

As for the fundamentals: GPU rental rates are firm. Powered shells are being leased as fast as they're built. To nitpick on one of our top holdings: at yesterday's close $WULF fell to $15, essentially at run-off value on three signed leases including the $19B Anthropic contract, and that's assuming the 10-year rises another 150bps to 6%! You are paying nothing for terminal value. The uncontracted pipeline (Hawesville's remaining ~79MW, Lake Mariner expansion, the new Cayuga site, and Morgantown, which FERC just approved July 29 up to 1GW), is also ours for free. A similar analysis applies to the other triple-net landlords in the space.

With both BTC and some of our highest-conviction names down 50%, we now think diversification is the wrong posture. We're going on offense.

Forced sellers create opportunities. This one had a name. Thanks Leo 🤝

It makes no sense to sum the net imho.

You either sum the losses to reflect actual pain locked in by investors, or you look at the net in raw form to assess regimes.

Studying the net is about regime change, and if you showed the positive values of your 1yr sum too, you'd see that the cross-overs occur when the bottom structure is well into forming (Dec 2018 and July 2022).

tweets.text: “One interesting tidbit is Alphabet had only $7.1 Billion quarterly depreciation expense with $321 Billion PP&E in 2Q’26. Meta, on the other hand, reported $6.4 Billion quarterly depreciation with just $226 Billion PP&E. So, Alphabet reported just ~$700 million incremental depreciation for almost $100 Billion incremental PP&E. I don’t know whether that speaks to Alphabet’s better efficiency of managing their PP&E or that Meta is too conservative in their estimates of useful life for its PP&E. Given how capital intensive these businesses are becoming, these arcane details can be very important over time which unfortunately would be hard to evaluate/judge from the outside.”
